title: Inorder Successor in BST
statement:
You are given `root`, the root of a binary search tree (every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's value, every value in its right subtree is larger, and no two nodes share a value), and a node `p` that belongs to the tree. Return the node visited immediately after `p` in an in-order traversal, which is the node whose value is the smallest one strictly greater than `p.val`. When `p` holds the largest value in the tree it has no successor, so return `null`.

Each case is written as `[root, p]`: the tree as a level-order array with `null` for missing children, followed by the value of `p`. Your function is called with the root and the node object `p` itself (not its value), must not change the tree, and must return a node of the tree or `null`; the result is shown as that node's `val`.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 10^4 nodes
root is a valid binary search tree
p is a node of the tree
notes:
## Intuition

The plain way is to list the whole tree in order and take the entry after `p`, which costs O(n) time and memory. The search-tree ordering lets us skip most of the tree. The successor is the smallest value above `p.val`, so walk down from the root as if searching for `p.val`. Whenever a node's value is larger than `p.val`, it is a candidate, and anything better must be smaller, so it lies to the left. Whenever the value is at most `p.val`, that node and its whole left subtree are too small, so go right. The last candidate seen is the answer.

## Approach

1. Start with `successor = null` and `node = root`.
2. While `node` is not `null`:
   - if `node.val > p.val`, record `node` as `successor` and move to `node.left`;
   - otherwise move to `node.right`.
3. Return `successor`, which stays `null` if no value was larger than `p.val`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree is `2` with children `1` and `3`, and `p` is the node `1`.

- At `2`: `2 > 1`, so `successor = 2` and the walk goes left to `1`.
- At `1`: `1 > 1` is false, so it goes right, to `null`.
- The loop ends and node `2` is returned.

In Example 2, `p = 6`: `5` is not larger, go right to `6`; `6` is not larger, go right to `null`. No candidate was recorded, so the answer is `null`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(h), where h is the tree's height: one step down per loop (O(n) for a chain, O(log n) when balanced).
- Space: O(1): only two variables.

## Pitfalls

- Use a strict `>`: when `node.val === p.val` the node is `p` itself, so the search must go right.
- Do not stop at the first larger node; a smaller candidate may still be in its left subtree.
- If `p` has a right subtree, the answer is the leftmost node there; if not, it is an ancestor. The single walk covers both cases, so no parent pointers are needed.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | root of the search tree |
| `p` | the node whose successor is wanted |
| `node` | the node the walk is currently at |
| `successor` | the smallest node above `p.val` found so far, or `null` |

narration.2: No node larger than p has been seen yet.
narration.3: Begin the walk at the root.
narration.4: Keep walking down until the path runs out.
narration.5: Is this node's value above p's? Then it could be the successor.
narration.6: It is the smallest larger value so far, because each candidate is smaller than the previous one.
narration.7: Anything closer to p.val must be smaller still, so look left.
narration.9: This node is p or smaller, so it and its left subtree are too small; look right.
narration.12: The last candidate recorded is the in-order successor, or null if there was none.
